segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Brothers and fathers, listen to the defense I now make before you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even quieter. And he said:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, trained according to the strictness of our ancestral law, and zealous for God, just as all of you are today.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I persecuted this Way to the death, binding both men and women and handing them over to prisons,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: as the high priest and the whole council of elders can testify for me. From them I also received letters to the brothers in Damascus, and I was on my way there to bring those who were there as well to Jerusalem in chains to be punished.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Now as I was on my way and getting near Damascus, about midday a great light from heaven suddenly flashed around me,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And he said to me,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Those who were with me saw the light but did not hear the voice of the one who was speaking to me.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I said, ‘What should I do, Lord?’ And the Lord said to me,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘Get up and go into Damascus, and there you will be told about everything that has been appointed for you to do.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Since I could not see because of the glory of that light, those who were with me led me by the hand, and so I came into Damascus.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: A certain Ananias, a man devout by the standard of the law and well spoken of by all the Jews living there,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: came to me, stood beside me, and said, ‘Brother Saul, see again!’ And at that very moment I could see again, and I looked up at him.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Then he said, ‘The God of our ancestors has appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One, and to hear a voice from his own mouth,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: because you will be his witness to all people of what you have seen and heard.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And now, why are you waiting? Get up, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on his name.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: After I had returned to Jerusalem, while I was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and saw him saying to me,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘Hurry, get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that I went from synagogue to synagogue imprisoning and beating those who believed in you.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by, approving, and guarding the cloaks of those who were killing him.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And he said to me,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They had been listening to him up to this statement, but then they raised their voices, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rid the earth of such a man! He should not be allowed to live!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were shouting, throwing off their cloaks, and flinging dust into the air,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: the commander ordered him to be brought into the barracks, saying that he should be examined by flogging, so that he could find out the reason they were shouting against him like this.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when they had stretched him out with the straps, Paul said to the centurion standing by,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and has not been condemned?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the centurion heard this, he went to the commander and reported it, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What are you about to do? This man is a Roman citizen.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The commander came and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Yes.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The commander answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I acquired this citizenship for a large sum of money.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “But I was born a citizen.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So those who were about to examine him drew back from him at once, and the commander himself was afraid when he realized that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had put him in chains.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The next day, wanting to know for certain what he was being accused of by the Jews, he released him and ordered the chief priests and the whole council to assemble. Then he brought Paul down and stood him before them.

notes.traditional: the Hebrew tongue / the Hebrew dialect
notes.note: The Greek phrase means the language of the Hebrews. Most scholars think this was Aramaic, the everyday language of Jewish Palestine, and some translations say 'Aramaic' outright. Others argue that Hebrew itself is meant. The literal wording is kept because the Greek does not settle the question.

notes.phrase: brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel
notes.traditional: brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel
notes.note: The Greek can be punctuated two ways. 'At the feet of Gamaliel' may go with 'brought up in this city', as here and in the SBLGNT punctuation, or with 'trained' ('educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strictness of our ancestral law'), as in many English versions. Either way Paul claims a Jerusalem upbringing and schooling under Gamaliel, a leading Pharisaic teacher.

'The Way' (literally 'the road') is the name Acts uses for the movement of Jesus's followers, apparently their own term for themselves. Paul uses it here without explanation, assuming the crowd knows which group he means.

The Greek does not name the town but uses a descriptive title, Nazōraios, attached to Jesus. Most translations render it 'of Nazareth', which is how it was generally understood. The form is kept as a title here because Acts later uses the same word in the plural for Jesus's followers (24:5).

Acts 9:7 says Paul's companions heard the voice, which seems to conflict with this verse. Some translations resolve the tension by rendering 'did not understand the voice' here, appealing to a difference in the grammatical case used with 'hear'. That distinction is disputed and not reliably observed in Greek of the period, so the plain rendering is kept.

notes.traditional: the Just One / the Righteous One
notes.note: This is a title for the Messiah, used also in Acts 3:14 and 7:52. Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice), so 'the Just One' translates the same word. Older versions use that form.

The Greek word is the ordinary one for a witness, the same word used of Paul himself in verse 15. The English 'martyr' derives from it, but the sense 'one who dies for the faith' developed later, partly from cases like Stephen's. Most modern translations render 'witness' here.

The same Greek word means 'nations' or 'peoples', and in the plural commonly refers to the non-Jewish peoples. English translations divide it between 'nations' and 'Gentiles' according to context. The crowd erupts at this word because of the claim that God was sending Paul away from Jerusalem to non-Jews.

The Greek title, literally 'commander of a thousand', was the standard equivalent of the Roman military tribune. This officer commanded the cohort garrisoned in the fortress beside the temple and is named in 23:26 as Claudius Lysias. English versions vary between 'tribune' and 'commander'.

notes.traditional: bound him with thongs / stretched him out for the whips
notes.note: The Greek word normally means a leather strap or thong. The phrase can mean that Paul was stretched out and tied with straps, as rendered here, or stretched out 'for the lashes', that is, for the whip. Translations are divided, and either way he is being positioned for the flogging ordered in verse 24.

'Roman' here means a holder of Roman citizenship, not a native of Rome. Roman law protected citizens from being bound or flogged without trial, and an officer who violated this could face serious consequences, which explains the commander's fear in verse 29. Citizenship could be inherited, granted, or, as the commander says of himself, obtained at considerable cost.

candidates.reason: Recurs through Acts 21–25 and in John, Mark and Revelation; translations split between 'tribune', 'commander' and 'captain', and readers would be confused if it varied.
Occurs across the Gospels and Acts, including of Jesus's followers in Acts 24:5; needs one decision between 'of Nazareth', 'the Nazarene' and 'the Nazorean'.
Frequent in the Gospels and Acts; translations alternate between 'council' and 'Sanhedrin', and the choice should be uniform.
The witness/martyr boundary (Acts 22:20; Revelation 2:13, 17:6) needs a single policy, along with the related μαρτυρέω and μαρτυρία.
As a name for the Jesus movement (Acts 9:2, 19:9, 19:23, 22:4, 24:14, 24:22) it needs a consistent capitalised rendering distinct from the ordinary sense 'road'.
